body.text: Australia and the US have made steady progress in military interoperability, but their next phase of cooperation should focus on how quickly they can generate, deploy and sustain a combined force. Linking rotational training with pre-positioned equipment, maintenance, fuel and distribution networks will turn the experience gained in exercises into a more enduring operational capability.

Following six months of training across Australia and the Indo-Pacific, the US 15th Marine Rotational Force-Darwin (MRF-D) deployment concluded on 23 October with a significant development in the Australia–US force posture relationship. For the first time in the program’s 14-year history, an MRF-D rotation was certified as a Special Purpose Marine Air-Ground Task Force, validating its ability to integrate command, ground combat, aviation and logistics capabilities for crisis response. As the US Marine Corps prepares for the 16th rotation to the Northern Territory in early 2027, the logistics arrangements supporting the force will need to keep pace with its growing operational reach.

The US Force Posture Initiative includes MRF-D and the Combined Logistics Sustainment and Maintenance Enterprise (CoLSME) supporting closer cooperation on logistics and sustainment. Pre-positioning equipment in Australia is an important part of this effort, but the ability to access and move the kit remains critical to its operational value.

Under CoLSME, US Army vehicles and equipment are stored at Bandiana in Victoria. The stock was reported in 2023 as around 330 vehicles and trailers , plus 130 containers. In Exercise Operose in 2024, some of the pre-positioned equipment was transported by road to Darwin. The exercise demonstrated the value of having materiel available in Australia, while highlighting the distances involved. The road journey is approximately 3,800 km and could take a convoy around 10 days, depending on the vehicles, route and movement arrangements. Partly because of the need for stops, military convoys move much more slowly than, commercial trucks.

A different approach was demonstrated during the 2024 Rapid Deployment Exercise, with US Marine Corps LAV-25 armoured reconnaissance vehicles flown from the US to the Royal Australian Air Force base at Edinburgh in Adelaide, then moved north by commercial rail. Transporting heavy equipment by rail is efficient, but the Adelaide–Darwin journey still spans thousands of kilometres and depends on the availability of the rail line, terminals and onward transport.

These examples illustrate a broader vulnerability addressed in my report, Making the littoral force operational: The logistics of Australia’s Northern Theatre. Australia’s northern force posture depends on transport links connecting southern equipment and supply hubs with forces operating in the north. Disruption to a critical route, or demand exceeding available capacity, could delay the movement of equipment and supplies. Having the capacity to move materiel efficiently in peacetime does not guarantee the redundancy or flexibility required during a crisis.

Retaining US MV-22B Osprey aircraft in Darwin between MRF-D rotations offers another way to sustain capability in the north. As reported in 2025, storing and maintaining the aircraft in Australia is intended to improve their availability for training, reduce transportation costs and remove import-related administrative burdens. Such arrangements reduce the effort required to re-establish capabilities for each rotation, although their longer-term value still depends on access to maintenance, fuel, skilled personnel and reliable distribution.

My explainer report, Closing the distance: Australia’s northern theatre logistics distribution gap, examines the wider challenge. Australia has substantial industrial and sustainment capacity, but much of it is concentrated in the south and southeast. Connecting that capacity to northern bases and operating areas requires reliable distribution networks, forward stockholding, repair and replenishment arrangements and infrastructure able to function under pressure.

For the Australian Defence Force and US forces, readiness depends on more than training personnel to operate together. It also relies on the ability to move equipment, access supplies, coordinate maintenance and sustain activity across dispersed locations.

Defence’s exploration of potential logistics hubs in Alice Springs and central Queensland provides an opportunity to improve how equipment and supplies are stored and moved to northern operating areas. The nodes should support Australia’s broader theatre logistics needs, while accommodating allied requirements where they align with national priorities and existing force posture arrangements.

Australia–US cooperation should be measured by how effectively forces can deploy, sustain and regenerate combat power when required, not only by the scale or complexity of their exercises. Connecting pre-positioned equipment and rotational training with resilient northern distribution networks would help ensure that the growing capability of MRF-D can be supported by the infrastructure needed to sustain operations across the Indo-Pacific.
